title: From Numerical Computation to Informatics Policy: Applied Mathematics and the Non-Aligned World in the ICC–IBI Transition (1951–1988)
content: The International Computation Centre (ICC) was established by a Convention signed in Paris on 6 December 1951 under UNESCO auspices and in force from 28 November 1961. Its preamble justified the Centre by “mathematical problems [...] which involve extremely complicated calculations”, and its Article II gave equal weight to research, education and a computation service. Transformed from 1969 and renamed the Intergovernmental Bureau for Informatics (IBI) in 1974, the organisation had 43 member states in 1985 and was dissolved in 1988. Historians have studied the genesis of the ICC and the information politics of the IBI separately; the place of applied mathematics across the transition has not been examined. I formulate three falsifiable hypotheses, define indicators and exact tests for them, and apply them to sources available online: the Convention and its ratification record in the UN Treaty Series, catalogue records of ICC and IBI symposia (1959–1974), the final report of the 1978 SPIN conference, the IBI’s 1985 self-presentation, its 1986 training plan, and data on membership of the Non-Aligned Movement (NAM). Three of the first eleven parties (1952–1962), including two of the ten whose acceptance brought the Convention into force, were founding NAM members. The ICC organised symposia on management and on the economics of data processing as early as 1965, alongside its mathematical meetings. In 1985, 34 of the 43 IBI member states were active NAM members and three were observers. Mathematical classes account for 3 of 6 classifiable units in 1959–1968 and none of 11 in 1978–1988 (two-sided Fisher exact test, p = 0.018); restricted to international conferences only, the difference is not significant (p = 0.17). Of the 77 activities in the IBI’s 1986 regional training plan, one concerns numerical analysis. The evidence points to a disciplinary shift, but a conclusive test will require work in the UNESCO Archives, which the paper specifies.
